A · What a Filter Is Key Terms — Saying What You Want

Filter

/ˈfɪl.tər/

Anything that changes how strong each frequency is. A decision about frequencies, carried out on samples.

สิ่งที่เปลี่ยนความแรงของแต่ละความถี่ — คือ "การตัดสินใจเรื่องความถี่" ที่ลงมือทำกับ sample

Passband / stopband

/ˈpɑːs.bænd/

The frequencies you keep, and the frequencies you remove.

ย่านที่เก็บไว้ (passband) กับย่านที่ตัดทิ้ง (stopband)

Cutoff frequency (fc​)

/ˈkʌt.ɒf/

The agreed border between keeping and removing. Usually quoted at −3 dB — but each library has its own convention, so measure it.

เส้นแบ่ง "เก็บ" กับ "ตัด" · ปกติวัดที่ −3 dB แต่แต่ละไลบรารีนิยามไม่เหมือนกัน — ต้องวัดเอง

Gain, in decibels

/ɡeɪn/ · dB

How much a frequency is multiplied by. 0 dB = unchanged · −20 dB = one tenth · −60 dB = one thousandth.

ตัวคูณของแต่ละความถี่ · 0 dB = เท่าเดิม · −20 dB = เหลือ 1/10 · −60 dB = เหลือ 1/1000

🔑

Sessions 6 and 7 gave you a way to see which frequencies are present. A filter is what you do next: decide which of them survive. Everything in this session is that one idea, built up carefully.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is Four shapes cover almost every job you will meet
🎛️

Read each picture as a sentence: "multiply every frequency by the height of this curve." Where the curve is at the top, the frequency passes untouched; where it is at the bottom, that frequency is gone. Naming the shape is the first half of specifying a filter — the cutoff is the other half.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is No filter is a cliff — so a spec needs three numbers
📐

A real filter slides from "keep" to "remove" over a transition band, so a usable spec says three things: the cutoff, how quickly it must fall, and how far down the stopband must be. And notice the number on the picture: this filter was asked for 1000 Hz and its −3 dB point measures 961 Hz — because firwin puts the −6 dB point where you asked. Measure, do not assume.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is The job picks the filter — not the other way round
🗣️

The useful skill is the translation: "the hum is at 50 Hz and my signal is above it" → highpass, cutoff below 50 · "speech lives between 300 and 3400 Hz" → bandpass with those edges. Get the sentence right and the code is one line.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is 🌍 Use case: the 50 Hz that is in every clinical recording
🏥

Mains wiring puts 50 Hz (or 60 Hz) into every sensitive recording ever made — ECG, EEG, microphones, strain gauges. Notice what the filter did not do: the R peaks are still where they were, at the heights they were. Removing one frequency is not the same as damaging the signal — provided the thing you removed was not part of it.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is ↩ What did the filter have to know?

Nothing about hum, and nothing about voices. The filter only ever knew three numbers about frequency — and none of them mention what the signal is.

That is why the same tool cleans an ECG, a phone call and a vibration sensor: you supply the meaning, the filter supplies the arithmetic.

⚠️

And it is why a filter can quietly destroy your data. If part of what you care about lives in the stopband, it is gone, and nothing in the output says so.

A · What a Filter Is 💻 LAB — Design four filters in four lines
①Ask for each shape by name · ② look at what came back · ③ read the cutoff off the plot
lab_a.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
fs = 8000
designs = {
    "lowpass" : signal.firwin(61, 800, fs=fs),
    "highpass": signal.firwin(61, 800, fs=fs, pass_zero=False),
    "bandpass": signal.firwin(61, [600, 1600], fs=fs, pass_zero=False),
}
for name, h in designs.items():
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, fs=fs)
    plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H)+1e-9), label=name)
plt.ylim(-80, 5); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.ylabel("dB"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
✅

Three curves with the shapes from slide 6. The lowpass and the highpass cross each other exactly at 800 Hz — both are 6 dB down there, which is where firwin puts the cutoff you ask for. And firwin returned 61 numbers: that list is the entire filter.

1 / 65
A · What a Filter Is 🔍 Explore — move the cutoff and watch the border move
explore_a.py
for fc in [200, 800, 2000, 3500]:
    h = signal.firwin(61, fc, fs=fs)
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=8192, fs=fs)
    db = 20*np.log10(abs(H)+1e-9)
    at3 = w[np.argmin(abs(db + 3))]              # the textbook cutoff
    at6 = w[np.argmin(abs(db + 6))]              # firwin's own convention
    print(f"asked {fc:5d} | -3 dB at {at3:7.1f} | -6 dB at {at6:7.1f}")
🔎

Measured: −3 dB at 151 · 747 · 1946 · 3447 Hz, but −6 dB at 202 · 800 · 2000 · 3500 Hz. So firwin hit the request exactly — at −6 dB, not −3. Neither convention is wrong; quoting one while your library uses the other is. It also promises nothing about how fast the curve falls afterwards: that is set by the number of taps (sub-topic C).

The thing in the middle is the entire filter. Where have you seen this operation before?

B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h Key Terms — The Filter Itself

FIR

/ˌef.aɪˈɑːr/ · Finite Impulse Response

A filter whose output is a weighted sum of the last N inputs. Feed it one spike and the answer stops after N samples — hence "finite".

ฟิลเตอร์ที่เอา input ย้อนหลัง N ตัวมาถ่วงน้ำหนักบวกกัน · ป้อน impulse เข้าไป ผลจะจบใน N sample

Taps / coefficients (h[k])

/tæps/

The list of weights. Choosing them is designing the filter — there is nothing else to choose.

ชุดตัวเลขน้ำหนัก · การเลือกค่าพวกนี้คือการออกแบบฟิลเตอร์ (ไม่มีอย่างอื่นให้เลือกแล้ว)

Impulse response

/ˈɪm.pʌls/

What comes out when you feed in a single 1. For an FIR filter it is exactly the taps — Session 3's h[n].

ผลลัพธ์เมื่อป้อน 1 ตัวเดียวเข้าไป · สำหรับ FIR มันคือ taps เป๊ะ ๆ (h[n] ของคาบ 3)

Order / length (N)

/ˈɔː.dər/

How many taps. More taps = a sharper filter and more arithmetic per sample.

จำนวน tap · มากขึ้น = ฟิลเตอร์คมขึ้น และคำนวณต่อ sample หนักขึ้น

🔑

Read the last two cards together: the filter, its taps and its impulse response are three names for the same list of numbers.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h This is Session 3, with the coefficients chosen on purpose
y[n]=∑k=0N−1​h[k]x[n−k]

"take the last N inputs, multiply each by its weight, add them up"

Session 3 wrote this and called it convolution.
Session 4 set every h[k] to 1/N and called it a moving average.
Session 8 asks the only question left: what if we choose the weights?

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h Four sets of taps, four different filters
🎯

Two of these you already know. All-equal taps average, and averaging removes high frequencies — that is column one. [1, −1] subtracts the previous sample, which only reacts when things change — a highpass, column two. Columns three and four were designed by a library, but they are the same kind of object: a short list of numbers.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h Session 4's moving average, seen from the frequency side
↩

In Session 4 we said the moving average "smooths". We can now say it precisely: it is a lowpass filter, and a longer window moves its cutoff down. That is the whole of this session in one sentence — the same operation, described in the language of frequency instead of the language of time.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h 🌍 Use case: where these lists of numbers actually run

🎧

Headphones

Noise cancelling runs a filter on the microphone signal thousands of times a second, on a chip the size of a grain of rice.

📷

Images

A blur kernel is a 2-D FIR filter, and the edge detector in your CV course is the [1, −1] of column two, in two directions.

📶

Every radio

Picking one station out of the air is a bandpass filter — the tuning knob moves its centre frequency.

🔗

The link to your other course is not a coincidence: convolution with a small kernel is the same operation in one dimension and in two. A CNN's first layer is a stack of learned FIR filters — the difference is that here you choose the taps, and there they are fitted from data.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h ↩ Where have you seen this operation before?

You have been running FIR filters since Session 3. Convolution is the machine; the taps are the instructions you give it.

What is new in this session is not the arithmetic — it is that we now choose h to get a stated effect on frequency, and can check that we got it.

💡

Which is also why "FIR" is not a scary word: if you can write a for-loop over a window, you can implement any FIR filter that exists.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h 💻 LAB — Prove the taps and the impulse response are the same list
①Design a filter · ② feed it a single 1 · ③ compare what comes out with the taps
lab_b.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

h = signal.firwin(7, 1000, fs=8000)
impulse = np.zeros(20); impulse[0] = 1

out = signal.lfilter(h, 1, impulse)          # run the filter on one spike
print("taps  ", np.round(h, 4))
print("output", np.round(out[:7], 4))
print("identical?", np.allclose(out[:7], h), "| zero after that?",
      np.allclose(out[7:], 0))
✅

Both prints show [0.0085 0.0698 0.245 0.3535 0.245 0.0698 0.0085] and then identical? True | zero after that? True. That "zero after that" is the F in FIR: the filter's memory of any one sample runs out after 7 steps.

1 / 65
B · FIR = Convolution with a Chosen h 🔍 Explore — three sets of taps, written by hand
explore_b.py
x = np.array([0,0,4,4,4,4,0,0,0], dtype=float)   # one step up, one step down
for name, h in [("average 3", np.ones(3)/3),
                 ("difference", np.array([1., -1.])),
                 ("pass-through", np.array([1.]))]:
    print(f"{name:12s}", np.round(np.convolve(x, h)[:9], 2))
🔎

Output — average 3: [0 0 1.33 2.67 4 4 2.67 1.33 0] · difference: [0 0 4 0 0 0 −4 0 0] · pass-through: the input, unchanged. Look at what each one reacted to: the average smeared the edges, the difference ignored the flat part entirely and marked only the two edges. Smoothing and edge-finding are the same operation with different weights.

🌍 In the real world

All three were asked for the same cutoff, and all three obeyed. So how do you say which one you actually wanted?

C · The Frequency Response Key Terms — Checking Before You Trust

Frequency response (H(f))

/rɪˈspɒns/

The gain the filter applies at every frequency — the curve you have been looking at all session.

ค่าที่ฟิลเตอร์คูณเข้าไปในแต่ละความถี่ — คือเส้นกราฟที่ดูกันมาทั้งคาบ

freqz

/frek-zed/

The one function that turns taps into that curve. Two lines of code, and it needs no input signal at all.

ฟังก์ชันที่เปลี่ยน taps เป็นเส้นกราฟ · ใช้สองบรรทัด และไม่ต้องมีสัญญาณจริงเลย

Ripple

/ˈrɪp.əl/

The small wobbles in the passband and stopband. Every real design has them; the question is how big.

คลื่นกระเพื่อมเล็ก ๆ ใน passband/stopband · ทุกดีไซน์จริงมี — คำถามคือใหญ่แค่ไหน

Attenuation

/əˌten.juˈeɪ.ʃən/

How far down the stopband sits, in dB. "−60 dB" means what is left is one thousandth of what came in.

ความลึกของ stopband เป็น dB · −60 dB = เหลือหนึ่งในพัน

🔑

The professional habit of this whole session: you do not learn what a filter does by running it on your data and squinting — you plot its response first, before any conclusion depends on it.

1 / 65
C · The Frequency Response The response is nothing new — it is Session 6 applied to h
🔗

Take the DFT of the impulse response and you have the frequency response. That is the entire definition — freqz is a convenience wrapper that picks the frequency points for you. Which also means the intuition runs both ways: a longer h gives finer frequency detail, for exactly the reason Session 6 gave — Δf=fs​/N.

1 / 65

—

🎚️

Every curve is a real firwin design computed at build time — the sliders pick between actual filters.

🔎

Move the first slider and the wall moves. Move the second and the wall gets steeper — while the taps above multiply.

C · The Frequency Response Taps buy sharpness — and you pay for them per sample

What more taps give you

A narrower transition band — the wall between keep and remove gets steeper.

What they cost you

N multiply-adds for every single output sample, and a delay of (N−1)/2 samples before you see the answer.

At fs​=44,100 Hz, a 501-tap filter is 22 million multiply-adds per second, per channel.

TapsTransition widthWork / sample
111468 Hz — very gradual11
31509 Hz31
101152 Hz — nearly a wall101
↩

Measured from the three curves that opened this sub-topic — so that is the answer to "which one did you actually want?": the one whose transition width your job needs, and no longer. Roughly, double the taps and the transition halves. There is no setting that gives a sharp filter for free.

1 / 65
C · The Frequency Response 🌍 Use case: predict first, then run — and check they agree
✅

The response said 300 Hz would pass at 0 dB and 2400 Hz would be cut by 66 dB. The measured output agrees. That agreement is the deliverable — in a report, "I filtered the data" is worth nothing next to "here is the response, here is the before, here is the after."

C · The Frequency Response 💻 LAB — Read three numbers off a response
①Design · ② find the cutoff · ③ measure the stopband floor and the transition width
lab_c.pyColab · no downloads needed
fs = 8000
h = signal.firwin(51, 1000, fs=fs)
w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=4096, fs=fs)
db = 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9)

cut   = w[np.argmin(abs(db + 3))]                 # the -3 dB point
stop  = db[w > 1600].max()                        # worst leak above 1600 Hz
trans = w[np.argmax(db < -40)] - cut               # how wide the ramp is
print(f"cutoff {cut:6.0f} Hz | stopband {stop:6.1f} dB | transition {trans:6.0f} Hz")
✅

cutoff   936 Hz | stopband  −55.1 dB | transition   304 Hz. Those three numbers are the filter, as far as anyone else is concerned. Put them in the caption of every filtered plot you publish.

1 / 65
C · The Frequency Response 🔍 Explore — what does doubling the taps actually buy?
explore_c.py
for N in [11, 21, 51, 101, 201]:
    h = signal.firwin(N, 1000, fs=fs)
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=4096, fs=fs)
    db = 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9)
    cut   = w[np.argmin(abs(db + 3))]
    trans = w[np.argmax(db < -40)] - cut
    print(f"N={N:4d} | transition {trans:6.0f} Hz | work/sample {N:4d}")
🔎

Transition widths: 1468 · 773 · 304 · 152 · 75 Hz. Read the pattern rather than the numbers — double the taps and the transition roughly halves, all the way down. So "how sharp do I need it?" is answered in taps, and taps are answered in CPU time. It is a straight purchase, and you should know the price before you sign.

D Sub-topic D · Linear Phase — the reason audio engineers reach for FIR
🌍 In the real world

Both filters removed the same frequencies. So why does only one of them still look like the input?

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase Key Terms — The Other Half of a Filter

Phase response

/feɪz/

How much each frequency is shifted in time. The response curve you have been reading only showed magnitude — this is the other half.

แต่ละความถี่ถูกเลื่อนเวลาไปเท่าไร · กราฟที่ดูมาทั้งคาบแสดงแค่ขนาด นี่คืออีกครึ่ง

Linear phase

/ˈlɪn.i.ər feɪz/

The phase line is straight, which means every frequency is delayed by the same number of samples.

เส้น phase เป็นเส้นตรง = ทุกความถี่ถูกหน่วงเท่ากันหมด

Symmetric taps

/sɪˈmet.rɪk/

h[k]=h[N−1−k] — the tap list reads the same forwards and backwards. This alone guarantees linear phase.

h[k] = h[N−1−k] · อ่านหน้าไปหลังกับหลังมาหน้าได้เหมือนกัน · แค่นี้ก็ได้ linear phase

Group delay

/ɡruːp dɪˈleɪ/

How long the filter holds the signal up: (N−1)/2 samples for a symmetric FIR. Known exactly, so it can be undone.

ฟิลเตอร์หน่วงสัญญาณนานเท่าไร = (N−1)/2 sample · รู้ค่าแน่นอน จึงหักลบคืนได้

🔑

So far, everything was about how loud each frequency comes out. This is about when — and getting it wrong changes a waveform's shape without changing one number in its spectrum.

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase Symmetric taps in, a straight phase line out
🪞

You can check this property by eye, on the coefficients, before running anything: if the list reads the same backwards, the phase is a straight line and every frequency is delayed identically. Every filter firwin produces is symmetric — that is a design choice the library made for you, and it is the main reason FIR filters are popular in audio.

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase The whole signal moves — and you know exactly how far
⏱️

A delay is only a problem when you do not know its size. Here you do: (N−1)/2 samples, the same for every frequency. So on recorded data you simply shift the result back and the alignment is perfect — that is what filtfilt does for you. In a live system you cannot shift back in time, and the delay becomes a real cost.

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase 🌍 Use case: three places where shape is the measurement

🫀

ECG

Diagnosis is made from the shape of the QRS complex and the spacing between waves. A filter that tilts the peaks has altered the evidence.

🎚️

Studio audio

Mastering engineers use linear-phase equalisers precisely so that changing the bass does not smear the transient of a drum hit.

📡

Data links

A receiver decides "1 or 0" from pulse shape. Smear the pulses into each other and the bit-error rate climbs.

🎧

The honest counterpoint: for listening, moderate phase distortion is close to inaudible, which is why cheap audio hardware uses IIR filters happily. Linear phase earns its cost when something downstream — a person reading a trace, or an algorithm measuring a pulse — depends on the shape rather than the sound.

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase ↩ Why does only one of them still look like the input?

A waveform is a sum of sinusoids (Session 5). Its shape comes from how those sinusoids line up in time.

Delay them all equally and they still line up — the picture just slides. Delay them by different amounts and they re-combine into a different shape, even though every magnitude is identical.

👻

Which is why this one is easy to miss: a magnitude plot cannot show it. Two filters can have identical response curves and do visibly different things to your data.

1 / 65
D · Linear Phase 💻 LAB — Check symmetry, then measure the delay
①Test h[k]=h[N−1−k] · ② send in a pulse · ③ find how far the peak moved
lab_d.pyColab · no downloads needed
h = signal.firwin(41, 1200, fs=8000)
print("symmetric?", np.allclose(h, h[::-1]))

n = np.arange(160)
x = np.exp(-(n - 40)**2 / 30)                       # one short pulse
y = signal.lfilter(h, 1, x)

print("peak in ", np.argmax(x), "| peak out", np.argmax(y),
      "| predicted shift", (len(h) - 1)//2)
✅

symmetric? True, then peak in 40 | peak out 60 | predicted shift 20. The prediction was made from the tap count alone — no signal required. A filter whose delay you can compute in your head is a filter you can align data with.

D · Linear Phase 🔍 Explore — break the symmetry on purpose
explore_d.py
good = signal.firwin(41, 1200, fs=8000)
bad  = good.copy(); bad[5] += 0.05          # nudge ONE tap

for name, h in [("symmetric", good), ("nudged", bad)]:
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=512, fs=8000)
    keep = abs(H) > 0.1              # phase is meaningless in the stopband
    ph = np.unwrap(np.angle(H[keep]))
    bend = np.abs(ph - np.linspace(ph[0], ph[-1], len(ph))).max()
    print(f"{name:10s} symmetric={np.allclose(h, h[::-1])!s:5s} "
          f"bend from a straight line = {bend:.2f} rad")
🔎

Result: symmetric → 0.00 rad — a perfectly straight phase, to floating-point precision — and nudged → 0.17 rad. One tap out of forty-one, changed by 0.05, and the exact guarantee is gone. Note the line that had to be there: phase is meaningless where the magnitude is ~0, so the test only looks at the passband. Measure it over the whole band and both filters look bent.

E · IIR, Stability and Choosing Key Terms — Filters That Remember

IIR

/ˌaɪ.aɪˈɑːr/ · Infinite Impulse Response

A filter that feeds its own output back in. One spike at the input can echo forever — hence "infinite".

ฟิลเตอร์ที่ป้อน output ของตัวเองกลับเข้าไป · ป้อน 1 ตัวเดียว ผลอาจไม่จบเลย

Feedback

/ˈfiːd.bæk/

Using y[n−1] to compute y[n]. That single move is the entire difference from FIR.

ใช้ y[n−1] มาคำนวณ y[n] · แค่นี้คือความต่างทั้งหมดจาก FIR

Difference equation

/ˈdɪf.rəns/

The recipe, written as one line: y[n]=b0​x[n]+b1​x[n−1]−a1​y[n−1]. It is already the code.

สูตรที่เขียนได้บรรทัดเดียว · เขียนแล้วแทบเป็นโค้ดอยู่แล้ว

Stability

/stəˈbɪl.ɪ.ti/

Whether that echo dies away or grows without limit. FIR filters cannot be unstable; IIR filters can.

เสียงสะท้อนจะค่อย ๆ หายไปหรือโตไม่หยุด · FIR ไม่มีทางพัง แต่ IIR พังได้

🔁

An echo in a room is the everyday version: the sound that comes back is part of what comes back next. If each reflection is a little quieter, it fades. If a microphone is pointed at its own speaker and each pass is a little louder, you get the screech everyone has heard — and that is an unstable filter, in a room.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing One extra term, and the filter gains a memory

FIR — looks only at the input

y[n]=b0​x[n]+b1​x[n−1]

IIR — also looks at what it just said

y[n]=b0​x[n]+b1​x[n−1]−a1​y[n−1]

Because y[n−1] contained y[n−2], which contained y[n−3], a single input sample can still be echoing thousands of steps later. That is where the efficiency comes from: the filter reuses work it has already done.

the difference equation is the code
y = np.zeros_like(x)
for n in range(1, len(x)):
    y[n] = 0.1*x[n] + 0.9*y[n-1]
💡

Three lines, and it is a working lowpass filter. Read it aloud: "keep 90% of what I said last time, and mix in 10% of what just arrived." Every smoothing routine you have ever seen in embedded code is this line.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing The price of feedback: it can run away
💥

The test is as simple as it looks: ∣a∣<1 and the echo dies; ∣a∣≥1 and it does not. Nothing warns you — the code runs, the numbers grow, and eventually you get infinities. An FIR filter cannot do this, because it has no memory of its own output to amplify.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing 🔭 One page on H(z) — the tool the textbooks use
H(z)=1+a1​z−1+…b0​+b1​z−1+…​=A(z)B(z)​

Take the difference equation and write z−1 wherever it says "one sample ago". The whole filter becomes one fraction: the b coefficients on top, the a coefficients underneath.

Zeros — where the top is 0 → frequencies the filter kills.
Poles — where the bottom is 0 → frequencies it boosts, and the source of all the trouble.

An FIR filter has A(z)=1 — no denominator, so no poles, so nothing that can blow up. That is the same fact as "FIR is always stable", said in the other language.

and you can just ask for them
z, p, k = signal.tf2zpk(b, a)
print("stable?", np.all(abs(p) < 1))
🔭

This is a two-page tour of a topic that is normally a whole course. You need it here for one thing only: the stability test on the next slide.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing 🔭 The whole stability rule, in one picture
🎯

Every pole inside the unit circle → stable. Any pole on or outside it → not. And notice the right-hand panel: the pole at 1.02 is barely outside, which is exactly the a=1.02 that ran away on slide 45. The picture and the ∣a∣<1 test are the same test — ∣a∣ is the distance of the pole from the centre.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing 🌍 Choosing: two questions settle almost every case
⚖️

① Does the shape of the waveform matter? Yes → FIR, for the straight phase line. ② Is the arithmetic budget tight — a microcontroller, a battery, a live loop? Yes → IIR, for the ten-numbers-instead-of-a-hundred. If both answers are yes you have a real engineering problem; if neither is, use FIR, because it cannot be unstable.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing ↩ What did the short one do differently?

It reused its own output. The past is already summarised in y[n−1], so it does not need to look back at a hundred raw samples to know what it said.

That is the same trick the FFT used in Session 7 — do not recompute what you already computed — and here it buys an order of magnitude.

💰

And it is paid for in two coins: the phase is no longer straight, and the filter can now be unstable. No free lunch, only a different bill.

E · IIR, Stability and Choosing 💻 LAB — Write an IIR filter in one line, then test it
①Write the loop by hand · ② check it against scipy · ③ ask whether it is stable
lab_e.pyColab · no downloads needed
x = np.zeros(50); x[0] = 1                     # one spike
a1 = 0.9

y = np.zeros_like(x)                        # the loop, by hand
for n in range(len(x)):
    y[n] = 0.1*x[n] + (a1*y[n-1] if n > 0 else 0)

ref = signal.lfilter([0.1], [1, -a1], x)          # the same thing, from scipy
print("match?", np.allclose(y, ref), "| y[0..3] =", np.round(y[:4], 4))
print("still ringing at n=49?", round(y[49], 6))
✅

match? True | y[0..3] = [0.1 0.09 0.081 0.0729] and still ringing at n=49? 0.000573. Each step is 0.9 of the one before — and fifty samples later it has still not reached zero. That is the "infinite" in IIR, and it is why an eleven-number filter can act like a hundred-tap one.

1 / 65
E · IIR, Stability and Choosing 🔍 Explore — walk a up to 1 and past it
explore_e.py
x = np.zeros(201); x[0] = 1                    # a longer run this time
for a1 in [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0, 1.01]:
    y = signal.lfilter([0.1], [1, -a1], x)
    z, p, k = signal.tf2zpk([0.1], [1, -a1])
    print(f"a={a1:5.2f} | |pole|={abs(p[0]):5.2f} | y[200]={y[-1]:12.4g}"
          f" | {'stable' if abs(p[0]) < 1 else 'UNSTABLE'}")
🔎

With 201 samples: a=0.50 → 6.2e−62 · 0.90 → 7.1e−11 · 0.99 → 0.0134 · 1.00 → 0.1 · 1.01 → 0.73. Read the fourth line carefully: at exactly a=1 the echo never fades and never grows — the filter has become a perfect accumulator. That is the knife edge, and real coefficients drift onto it through rounding. Which is why the rule is ∣a∣<1, strictly.

🎯 The brief: fs​=8000 Hz, lowpass at 800 Hz, running live on a small microcontroller.

# TODO 1: design signal.firwin(101, 800, fs=8000) and
#         signal.butter(4, 800, fs=8000, btype="low"); plot both responses

# TODO 4: two sentences — which would you ship for this brief, and what
#         would change your mind?
✅

The IIR needs 9 multiply-adds against the FIR's 101, and its poles have magnitudes 0.795 and 0.544 — comfortably inside the circle, so stable. Its phase bends; the FIR's is straight. For this brief — live, small chip, audio — ship the IIR. What would change your mind: if the output feeds a peak-shape measurement rather than a listener, or if the chip has a hardware multiply-accumulate that makes 101 taps free anyway.

"Can I pull my own heartbeat out of a phone-camera video of my fingertip?"

Average the red channel per frame · bandpass 0.7–3 Hz · count the peaks and compare with a real pulse reading.

Spectrum first to find its band · design a bandstop · report the level before and after, in dB.

Lowpass to kill the hand tremor · highpass to kill gravity · count peaks and compare with a manual count.

What a good report contains: the response of the filter you used with its cutoff and its length stated, the signal before and after, and one number that got better — a noise level, an error count, a correlation. A picture of a cleaner-looking waveform is not evidence on its own.

🧮Worked Example — Turning a Complaint into a Filter Spec

Given

  • "My EEG recording is unreadable — there is mains buzz all over it."
  • fs = 500 Hz · mains = 50 Hz
  • Brain rhythms of interest: 1–40 Hz

Find

  • shape, cutoff(s), and one sentence of justification
Shapethe junk sits above everything wanted → lowpass
Cutoffabove 40, below 50 → pick 45 Hz
Checkis 45 Hz below fs/2 = 250? ✓ (Session 2)
Steepnessonly 5 Hz between keep and kill → it must be sharp
∴ lowpass, fc = 45 Hz, and long enough to fall 40 dB in 5 Hz
⚠️

A bandstop at 48–52 Hz is the other valid answer, and it is better if you also need the band above 50. The wrong answer is not choosing — a 5 Hz gap is expensive, and you should notice that before you design.

1 / 65
✎Quick Check — Name That Filter⏱ 2 min

A response is flat at 0 dB from 0 to 300 Hz, falls to −40 dB by 900 Hz, and stays there. (a) What shape is it? (b) Roughly where is the cutoff? (c) A 600 Hz tone goes in at amplitude 1. Roughly what comes out?

✅

(a) Lowpass. (b) The −3 dB point is just past 300 Hz, so the cutoff is around 350 Hz — read it off the curve, do not guess it from the middle of the slope. (c) At 600 Hz the curve is at about −20 dB, which is a factor of ten: amplitude ≈ 0.1. Note it is not zero — "in the stopband" never means "gone", it means "small enough".

1 / 65
🧮Worked Example — One FIR Output, by Hand

Given

  • h = [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]
  • x = [0, 4, 8, 4, 0, 0]

Find

  • y[2] and y[3]
  • the delay this filter adds
  • its gain at 0 Hz, without any transform
y[2]0.25(8) + 0.5(4) + 0.25(0) = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4
y[3]0.25(4) + 0.5(8) + 0.25(4) = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6
Delaysymmetric, N = 3 → (3−1)/2 = 1 sample
DC gainsum of taps = 0.25+0.5+0.25 = 1 → constants pass unchanged
∴ y[2] = 4 · y[3] = 6 · delayed by 1 · DC gain 1
🔑

Two free checks you can do on any tap list without a computer: read it backwards (symmetric → linear phase) and add it up (sum = DC gain).

1 / 65
✎Quick Check — Will This One Blow Up?⏱ 3 min

A colleague sends you three one-line filters. Which of them are safe to run, and how do you know without running any of them?

✅

① safe — the feedback coefficient is 0.8 and |0.8| < 1, so each echo is smaller than the last. ② unsafe — |−1.1| > 1, so every pass is 10% louder and it grows without limit. ③ safe, and not even a question — look carefully: there is no y[n−1] term at all, so it is an FIR filter, and no FIR filter can be unstable.

Part B 💻 In code — Q5 (the filter chain you would actually ship)

Topics pulled in: filter shapes · taps and sharpness · linear phase and delay · FIR vs IIR

📋The Case — A Wrist Heart-Rate Monitor

The situation

  • An optical sensor on the wrist samples at fs = 100 Hz.
  • A heartbeat is 0.7–3 Hz (42–180 bpm).
  • The signal drifts slowly as the strap shifts: below 0.5 Hz.
  • Arm movement adds bursts above 5 Hz.
  • It runs on a coin cell, and must show the rate live.

Answer these

  • Q1 — which filter shape removes both problems at once, and with what edges?
  • Q2 — an FIR at this fs​ needs about 301 taps to be sharp enough. What delay is that, in seconds?
  • Q3 — is that delay acceptable for a live heart-rate display? Say why.
  • Q4 — FIR or IIR for this product? Give the two reasons that decide it.
💭

Work in order: what to remove → what shape → how sharp → what that costs in delay and arithmetic → which technology fits the product.

✔Part A — Answers
Q1Drift is below the beat, movement is above it → bandpass, about 0.5–5 Hz.
One filter, both problems, because the wanted band sits between them.
Q2(301−1)/2 = 150 samples ÷ 100 Hz = 1.5 seconds.
Q3Borderline, and probably not. The number on the screen would be describing
your heart 1.5 s ago — harmless while resting, wrong during intervals.
Q4IIR. ① The battery: ~10 numbers per sample instead of 301.
② Nothing here reads waveform shape — we only count peaks — so the
bent phase costs nothing. Both of the FIR's advantages are irrelevant here.
🧠

Q4 is the habit to carry into the project: the right filter is not the best filter, it is the one whose costs your application does not care about. Change the product to a clinical ECG that a cardiologist reads, and the same reasoning flips to FIR.

💻Q5 — The Filter Chain You Would Ship
case.pyfill in the TODOs
fs = 100
# build a stand-in: 30 s of a 1.2 Hz pulse + 0.2 Hz drift + bursts at 8 Hz
# TODO 1: design signal.butter(4, [0.5, 5], fs=fs, btype="band")
# TODO 2: check stability with tf2zpk — print max |pole|
# TODO 3: plot the response, and the signal before and after
# TODO 4: count peaks in the filtered signal (scipy.signal.find_peaks)
#         and convert to bpm. How close is it to 1.2 Hz = 72 bpm?
# TODO 5: repeat with filtfilt instead of lfilter. What changed about the
#         peak TIMES, and why can a real watch not do this?
✅

Expected: max |pole| ≈ 0.98 — stable, but close to the edge, which is normal for a narrow low-frequency band and a good reason to use sos form in production. The drift and the bursts both vanish, and the peak count gives ≈ 72 bpm. With filtfilt the peaks land at the true times because the delay cancels — and a watch cannot do it, because filtering backwards requires data from the future.
